Dear Mr. Harris: 
We write regarding the amicus brief filed by the Coalition of Large Tribes (COLT) in the case Suncor 
v. Boulder County, No. 25-170, on May 21, 2026.  Our client, COLT, is an intertribal Section 17 
corporation chartered by the Department of the Interior as an advocacy organization to represent the 
interests of the more than 50 tribes with reservations of 100,000 acres or more.  COLT’s enumerated 
purposes include, among others, “Educating the Administration, Congress, public and other tribes 
about the unique issues impacting tribes that govern large land bases;” and “Advocating for the exercise 
of tribal sovereignty and juri sdiction to the fullest extent including the sovereign right to develop 
natural resources, pursue agricultural efforts and develop and enhance Reservation infrastructure such 
as transportation and water infrastructure.”  Article 8, COLT Charter.  COLT operates under the 
unanimous action of its Board, comprised of Voting Member Tribes, as set forth in COLT’s Charter 
and Bylaws approved by the Secretary of the Interior.
COLT has endeavored to file an amended brief with the Court that removes two references to the 
Southern Ute Indian Tribe.  Following the filing of the brief in May, the Southern Ute Indian Tribe in 
late July requested that COLT remove the brief's limited factual references to the Southern Ute Indian 
Tribe, which is not a COLT member. Although the references were accurate background information 
about a large land base tribe and were not material to any legal argument presented by COLT, COLT 
agreed to accommodate the request as a matter of intertribal comity. Accordingly, COLT respectfully 
requests leave to substitute the attached corrected brief, which removes those references while leaving 
all substantive legal arguments, authorities, and positions unchanged. 
If you are able to include such a brief on the docket, COLT would appreciate your so doing. If you are 
not able to do so, this letter should serve as notice to clarify that the Southern Ute Indian Tribe does 
not embrace COLT’s position in this case.

To be absolutely clear, the filing of the COLT brief was as-directed by unanimous action of the COLT 
Board at two meetings with quorums present and considerable additional discussions over six 
months. While COLT respects the rights of every tribe to take any position it feels best serves its 
sovereign interests, COLT’s position as an intertribal Section 17 corporation is as set forth in the 
amended amicus brief as unanimously directed by the COLT Board. 
Very respectfully,
